old: Work of 23 to 25 November 2026, rewritten on 25 November to be shorter and plainer.
why: Housekeeping. A stranger does not need the page's history before its first sentence, and the fold's own first lines already say the page was rewritten.

old: Three planets would be nearly as good as new
why: With fig-up-b, moves the heading from above the figure to below it, so that the figure stands under the opening paragraph. The picture answers the opening question for all seven bodies and its loudest feature is the Moon; under a heading about three planets it seems to contradict the heading (Jupiter, a 'good' planet, is 6.4 degrees out and Saturn, a 'bad' one, 2.6).

old: The front dial on 23 November 2026, if the machine had been kept turning since 205 BC. Each ring is one body, from the Moon at the centre out to Saturn. The blue dot is where the pointer would stand and the orange ring is where the body really is, both measured against the stars.
new: The front dial on 23 November 2026, if the machine had been kept turning since 205 BC (why that year is told below). Each ring is one body: from the centre outwards, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The blue dot is where the pointer would stand and the orange ring is where the body really is, both measured against the stars. On this one day the Moon's pointer would be 105° from the Moon, and each of the others within 7° of its body.
why: 205 BC first turns up here with nothing to say what it is, two lines after 'a shipwreck of the first century BC', and is explained four sections later; the bracket tells the reader an answer is coming. The caption also did not say what to see; the one sentence that does was hidden in the alt text. The names in the picture stand in a column far from the dots (I gave Jupiter's pair to Saturn at first) and cannot be read at all on a phone, so the order of the rings is spelt out; it is the order of the labels in the figure. 'On this one day' warns that the picture is a single day, which the text's 'typical error' and 'at times 35°' otherwise leave the reader to work out.

new: Three planets would be nearly as good as new
why: Second half of the heading move (see fig-up-a). 'Start with the surprise.' goes: the heading now sits directly above and says it, and the sentence would be wrong if the Moon section is moved ahead of this one, as the report recommends.

old: Their typical error has grown by between 11% and 22% in more than two thousand years.
new: Their typical error has grown by between 11% and 22%.
why: The span of time was carrying four different expressions (two thousand two hundred years, more than two thousand years, two thousand years, 2,231 years). Here it is not needed: the sentence before says 'today as when the machine was new'.

old: Beside errors of that size, two thousand years of slow drift in the gears add little. The pointers for Venus and Saturn have gear ratios that are less good, and there the drift does show: Venus is now typically seven times as far out as at the start, and Saturn nearly twice.
new: Beside errors of that size, the slow drift that comes from the gear ratios adds little, even in two thousand two hundred years. The ratios for Venus and Saturn are less good, and there the drift does show: the pointer for Venus is now typically seven times as far out as at the start, and the pointer for Saturn nearly twice.
why: 'Drift in the gears' reads as wear or slipping, and the page later says 'I assumed perfect gears'. The story itself puts the drift down to the gear ratios (next sentence, and the Moon paragraph), so it is said so here. The span is given in the opening paragraph's words. It is the pointers that are out, not Venus and Saturn.

old: One thing has to be said about all five.
why: Shorter, and tells the reader what kind of thing is coming.

old: The ratios are those of a reconstruction published by Freeth and others in 2021, and for the three planets that do well they are that paper's restoration, not numbers read on the machine.
new: The gear ratios I used are those of a reconstruction published by Freeth and others in 2021, and for the three planets that do well they were supplied by that paper, not read on the machine.
why: 'Reconstruction' and 'restoration' in one sentence looked like two names for one thing, or two things I could not tell apart. 'Supplied by that paper' is what I took 'that paper's restoration' to mean. (See needs-author venus-saturn for the half of this that the story leaves out.)

old: The Moon would be a third of a turn out
new: The Moon would be nearly a third of a turn out
why: The paragraph says 'nearly a third'; the heading and the text should give the one figure.

old: The Moon is another matter. Its gears give it 254 turns in 19 years, which is slow against the stars by 0.12° a year.
new: The Moon's gears give it 254 turns in 19 years, a ratio that runs slow against the stars by 0.12° a year.
why: Introduces the word 'ratio' by an example, which the page otherwise uses unexplained. The opening 'The Moon is another matter' is dropped so that the paragraph reads right whether this section stays where it is or moves ahead of the planets; the heading makes the turn in either case.

old: The machine's theory of the Moon was good to about a degree, so here it is the gears that fail, and their drift overtook the theory's error within nine years.
new: The machine's picture of how the Moon moves was good to about a degree, so it is the gear ratio that fails: its slow running added up to more than that within nine years.
why: I read this sentence three times. 'Theory' here and 'picture of the heavens' in the planets section are one notion under two names; 'picture' is the plainer. 'The gears that fail' sits badly with 'I assumed perfect gears'; the sentence before says it is the ratio that is slow. 'Here' is dropped so that the sentence stands in either order of the sections.

old: The eclipse dial would have worked for centuries
new: The eclipse dial would have gone on marking real eclipses for centuries
why: 'Worked' promises more than the section delivers: it counts marked months that held an eclipse, counts them generously (its own word), and says the dial also came to miss eclipses. This says what was counted and no more.

old: How many of the dial's marked months still held an eclipse, one step for each eighteen-year cycle. Once a line reaches zero it stays there.
new: How many of the dial's marked months still held an eclipse, one step for each eighteen-year cycle. The dashed line leaves out eclipses of the Moon too faint to notice. Once a line reaches zero it stays there.
why: The picture has three lines and the text explains the third only three paragraphs further down; on a phone the legend inside the picture is too small to read. The wording is the legend's and the later paragraph's. If the dashed line is taken out of the story's figure, as the report suggests, drop this sentence again.

old: The cause is a slip of about half a degree in each cycle against the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's, near which every eclipse happens.
new: The cause is a slip. Every eclipse happens near one of the two points where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's, and each cycle slips about half a degree against those points.
why: The sentence made the reader hold 'a slip ... against the two points' before knowing what the points are or why they matter. Now the points come first and the slip second; nothing is added.

old: So the marks go stale from one edge, and a month that has lost its eclipse never gets one back.
new: So the marks go stale, and a month that has lost its eclipse never gets one back.
why: 'From one edge': edge of what? Nothing in the story says. Cut here; needs-author one-edge has a version that explains it with a fact from the fold.

old: Everything above starts the dial in 205 BC, because three published studies put its first full moon on 12 May of that year.
new: Everything above has the machine turning from 205 BC, because three published studies put the first full moon of its eclipse dial on 12 May of that year.
why: 'The dial' has meant the front dial (first figure) and the eclipse dial by turns, and 'everything above' includes the pointers on the front. The caption's own words are that the machine is kept turning since 205 BC; the dial whose first full moon is meant is named.

old: the hours fit four of the sixteen, the starts of 223, 205, 187 and 169 BC, which are one eighteen-year cycle apart. The cycle is about a third of a day longer than a whole number of days, so each of the four fits at a place about a third of the way round the world from the one before.
new: the hours fit four of the sixteen, the starts of 223, 205, 187 and 169 BC, each at a place about a third of the way round the world from the one before.
why: The hardest sentence on the page, and it explains the wrong thing: why the places are a third of the world apart, when what a stranger lacks is why hours should fit 'at a place' at all. The reason (a third of a day, the eighteen-year spacing) is for a checker and is already under the fold in 'The hours'. The fact itself is kept. See needs-author hours-place for a version that explains.

old: Carman and Evans had shown that a scheme like this one drifts and has to be reset, and how the hours fix the year.
new: Carman and Evans had shown that a scheme like the dial's drifts and has to be reset, and how the hours fix the year.
why: 'This one' has nothing near it to point at; the last scheme mentioned is the argument from the hours.

old: Their reports, and what I got wrong, are at the foot of the page. They share my training and may share my blind spots.
new: Those copies share my training and may share my blind spots. Their reports, and what I got wrong, are at the foot of the page.
why: As it stood, 'They share my training' followed 'Their reports' and read for a moment as if the reports shared the training. Same two sentences, in the other order.
